blocks.text: **Sorting** means putting items in order by some **key** — numbers from smallest to largest, names alphabetically, orders by date. It's the most used algorithm in programming, and in interviews it's one of the most useful tricks: once data is sorted, a hard question often becomes an easy scan.

blocks.text: Sorted data has structure that unsorted data doesn't, and many algorithms depend on it:

items: **Searching** — binary search finds a value among a million sorted values in about 20 steps instead of a million.
**Duplicates and groups** — equal values end up **next to each other**, so one pass finds duplicates or counts groups.
**Two pointers** — pairs with a target sum, closest pairs and merging all rely on order to know which pointer to move.
**Intervals and schedules** — sorting meetings by start time lines up overlaps so one scan can merge or count them.
**Everyday software** — database `ORDER BY`, leaderboards, file listings and search results are all sorts.
**Comparison sort** — decides the order only by comparing two items at a time (`a < b`). Bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick and heap sort all work this way.
**Non-comparison sort** — uses the values themselves as positions, like counting how many of each number there are. Counting, radix and bucket sort.
**In-place** — needs only O(1) extra memory besides the array itself.
**Stable** — items with **equal keys keep their original order**. This matters when you sort by one key after another (by name, then by grade).
**Adaptive** — runs faster when the input is already nearly sorted.

blocks.text: The speed limit: O(n log n)

No comparison sort can beat **O(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case. There are n! possible orders of n items, and each comparison has two outcomes, so at best it rules out half of the orders still possible. Telling all n! apart needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons — about **n log₂ n**. Merge sort and heap sort reach that limit; the simple sorts take O(n²). Only non-comparison sorts go faster, and they need extra facts about the values (small integers, a fixed number of digits).

You'll rarely write a sort from scratch at work — every language has a fast, well-tested one. Know how to call it, and how to pass your own **comparator**: a function that returns a negative number when `a` should come first, a positive one when `b` should, and 0 when they're equal.

blocks.code:
def sort_numbers(nums):
    return sorted(nums)                   # sorted() returns a new list; nums.sort() sorts in place

blocks.text: Sorting by a key looks the same in every language — tell the sort what to compare:

blocks.code:
JavaScript  people.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age)
Python      people.sort(key=lambda p: p.age)
Java        people.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(p -> p.age))
C++         sort(people.begin(), people.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) { return a.age < b.age; })

blocks.text: The rest of this introduction opens up the classic algorithms one at a time — each drawn, simulated and timed — so you know what these built-ins do and when to write your own.

items: Sorting arranges items by a **key**; once sorted, duplicates sit together and binary search and two pointers work.
Comparison sorts can't beat **O(n log n)**; counting and radix sort can, by using the values themselves.
**Stable** keeps equal keys in their original order; **in-place** uses O(1) extra memory.
In JavaScript, always give `sort` a comparator for numbers — the default compares them as text.
